claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has approximately 20 at.% each of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti.
As-cast equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
This starting state has favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength.
The low hardness and strength are governed by the alloy's simple single-phase solid-solution state.
The single-phase state contains little or no short-range chemical ordering or nanoscale precipitation.
The absence of short-range order and nanoscale precipitates leaves dislocation glide essentially unimpeded.
A controlled heat treatment can induce nanoscale Ti-rich precipitates without changing the overall CoCrFeNiTi composition.
The induced nanoscale precipitates or localized short-range-ordered regions serve as dislocation pinning sites.
In the as-cast CoCrFeNiTi state, relatively free dislocation glide enables efficient dynamic recovery.
Efficient dynamic recovery produces low work hardening and limited strength in the as-cast alloy.
Fine precipitates increase barriers to dislocation motion through pinning or dislocation bowing and bypass.
Precipitate-induced restriction of glide will increase the yield strength of CoCrFeNiTi.
Precipitate-induced restriction of glide will increase the hardness of CoCrFeNiTi.
Precipitate-induced restriction of glide will increase the work-hardening rate of CoCrFeNiTi.
Heat-treated samples will contain discrete nanoscale precipitates associated with dislocation pile-ups or other evidence of impeded dislocation motion.
The controlled comparison uses identical feedstock and compares an untreated as-cast group with a heat-treated group.
Mechanical testing is restricted to room-temperature, quasi-static loading.
The hypothesis is restricted to near-equimolar, conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi without martensitic transformation or major grain coarsening during testing.
Failure to observe statistically significant increases in yield strength, hardness, and work-hardening rate is proposed as a falsification outcome.
Failure to produce distinguishable precipitates is proposed as falsifying the dislocation-pinning hypothesis.
